questions.title: Erythropoiesis — where mitosis is lost
questions.question: In erythropoiesis, mitosis (proliferation) is lost in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The CFU-erythrocyte (colony-forming unit) is an early committed progenitor, well before the mitotic capacity of the maturing erythroid series is lost.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The basophilic erythroblast is still an actively dividing stage, earlier in the series than the point where mitosis is lost.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The proerythroblast is the very first recognisable precursor and is still capable of mitosis; it is far too early in the series for mitosis to have been lost already.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The polychromatophilic erythroblast is in fact the LAST stage still capable of mitosis, not the stage where that capacity is lost; it is the stage immediately before the one this question is asking for.
explanations.E: Correct. Mitosis (the capacity to divide) is lost at the normoblast stage, the stage immediately after the polychromatophilic erythroblast, which is the last dividing stage. From the normoblast onward the erythroid series only matures — condensing its nucleus and extruding it — without further cell division.

questions.learning_objective: State that the normoblast is the first erythroid stage to have lost the capacity for mitosis, immediately after the last dividing stage (the polychromatophilic erythroblast).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.16

questions.title: Term for decreased RBC count
questions.question: Decreased RBCs count is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Polycythemia is the opposite term — an INCREASED RBC count, not a decreased one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leukemia is a malignant proliferation of white blood cells; it is not the term for a decreased red cell count.
explanations.C: Correct. A decreased RBC count is called anemia. It may arise from decreased production (for example bone marrow depression), increased loss (haemorrhage) or increased destruction (haemolysis) of red cells, but the term itself simply names the reduced count and the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity that follows from it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leukopenia is a decreased white blood cell count, not a decreased red cell count.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia is a decreased platelet count, a different cell line from the erythrocyte this question is asking about.

questions.learning_objective: Name anemia as the term for a decreased RBC count, as distinct from leukopenia (white cells) and thrombocytopenia (platelets).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.16

questions.title: What erythropoiesis means
questions.question: Erythropoiesis means the development of:

explanations.A: Correct. Erythropoiesis is the term for the development (production and maturation) of red blood cells. It runs from the proerythroblast through several intermediate erythroblast stages and the reticulocyte to the mature erythrocyte. The name itself builds on "erythro-", the same root used for the mature red cell it produces.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphocyte development is not called erythropoiesis; lymphocytes arise from the separate lymphoid line.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Monocyte development is part of the myeloid (granulocyte-monocyte) line, not the erythroid line erythropoiesis names.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basophil development is part of granulopoiesis, the granulocyte series, not erythropoiesis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Eosinophil development is likewise part of granulopoiesis, not erythropoiesis.

questions.learning_objective: Define erythropoiesis as the development of red blood cells, as distinct from the separate lymphoid and granulocyte-monocyte lines.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.18

questions.title: Main site of erythropoiesis in middle age
questions.question: The main site of erythropoiesis in middle age is:

explanations.A: Correct. By middle age, as through the rest of adult life, red bone marrow is the main site of erythropoiesis. It persists specifically in the membranous bones — vertebrae, skull, ribs, pelvis and sternum — once the marrow of the long bone shafts has converted to inactive yellow marrow. The earlier fetal sites (yolk sac, liver, spleen) have long since handed over to this adult one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity surrounds the developing embryo/fetus in fluid; it is not, and has never been, a site of blood cell formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The yolk sac is the site of erythropoiesis only in the earliest weeks of embryonic life, not in middle age; erythropoiesis moves on from the yolk sac to the liver, spleen and finally bone marrow well before birth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lymph node is a site of lymphocyte proliferation and immune surveillance, not a site of erythropoiesis at any age.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lung has no haemopoietic function at any stage of life.

questions.learning_objective: State that red bone marrow of the membranous bones is the main erythropoietic site by middle age and throughout adult life.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.18

questions.title: Erythropoiesis — where haemoglobin starts to appear
questions.question: During erythropoiesis, hemoglobin starts to appear in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The basophilic erythroblast's cytoplasm is still purely basophilic (ribosome-rich, blue-staining on Romanowsky stain), which is why it is named for basophilia rather than for any visible haemoglobin yet.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The CFU-erythroid is an early committed progenitor, well before any visible haemoglobin content, since it precedes even the first recognisable erythroblast stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By the reticulocyte stage haemoglobin synthesis is already essentially complete, one stage further on than where it FIRST becomes visible.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haemoglobin synthesis is not complete until the normoblast stage, but it has already started appearing one stage earlier, at the polychromatophilic erythroblast.
explanations.E: Correct. Haemoglobin starts to appear at the polychromatophilic erythroblast stage. This stage is literally named for its mixed ("polychromatic") staining — a cytoplasm that is part basophilic (residual ribosomal RNA, blue) and part acidophilic (the newly accumulating haemoglobin, pink) — which is the visible sign that haemoglobin synthesis has begun.

questions.learning_objective: State that haemoglobin first becomes visible at the polychromatophilic erythroblast stage, one stage before its synthesis completes at the normoblast.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.19

questions.title: Term for increased RBC count
questions.question: Increased RBCs count is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anemia is the opposite term — a DECREASED RBC count, not an increased one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leukopenia is a decreased white blood cell count, a different cell line from the erythrocyte this question is asking about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thrombocytopenia is a decreased platelet count, again a different cell line.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leukocytosis is an increased white blood cell count, not an increased red cell count.
explanations.E: Correct. An increased RBC count is called polycythemia, up to roughly 6-8 million/mm3. It may be primary, arising from the bone marrow itself (polycythemia vera), or secondary, driven by tissue hypoxia stimulating erythropoietin.

questions.learning_objective: Name polycythemia as the term for an increased RBC count, and distinguish primary from secondary causes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.19

questions.title: Site of erythropoiesis in the early embryo
questions.question: Site of erythropoiesis in early embryo is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The liver becomes the major site of fetal erythropoiesis a little later, after the yolk sac stage, not in the earliest embryo.
explanations.B: Correct. In the early embryo, erythropoiesis begins in the yolk sac mesoderm, the earliest of the sites the erythropoietic function shifts through with age. This yolk sac phase lasts only a few weeks before the site of erythropoiesis moves on, first to the liver and spleen and eventually to bone marrow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Red bone marrow becomes active only later in fetal life and remains the site through childhood and adulthood; it is not where erythropoiesis begins in the earliest embryo.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spleen becomes a site of fetal erythropoiesis after the yolk sac and alongside the liver, not at the very start.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Yellow bone marrow is inactive, fatty marrow, the opposite of an active erythropoietic site at any stage.

questions.learning_objective: State that erythropoiesis begins in the yolk sac mesoderm in the early embryo, before shifting to the liver, spleen and finally bone marrow.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.19

questions.title: Duration of yolk sac hematopoiesis (past-exam block, دفعة 63)
questions.question: Hematopoiesis in the yolk sac of the embryo continues for:

explanations.A: Correct. Yolk sac haematopoiesis is brief, lasting only a few weeks of early embryonic life. After that short window, the site of blood cell formation shifts on to the liver and spleen. Bone marrow only becomes the dominant site later still, in the third trimester and beyond.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Yolk sac activity has already ended well before the end of the second trimester; by then the liver and spleen (and increasingly bone marrow) have taken over.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third trimester's dominant haemopoietic site is bone marrow, not the long-since-inactive yolk sac.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Yolk sac haematopoiesis is confined to early embryonic life; it plays no role anywhere near puberty.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The yolk sac's haemopoietic role is the shortest-lived of all the sites in the sequence, not a lifelong one; bone marrow is the site that persists lifelong instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that yolk sac haematopoiesis lasts only a few weeks of early embryonic life before the site shifts to the liver, spleen and bone marrow.
